hints: Work out the oxidation number change for Cl in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ to $\text{ClO}_2$ and for S in $\text{SO}_2$ to $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ to see how many of each species must combine.
walkthrough:
Track the oxidation numbers**
Think with me about what is reduced and what is oxidised. In $\text{ClO}_3^-$, Cl is +5, in $\text{ClO}_2$ it is +4, so each Cl gains 1 electron. In $\text{SO}_2$, S is +4, in $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ it is +6, so each S loses 2 electrons.

Balance electrons then atoms**
One S gives 2 electrons, so you need two Cl atoms each accepting 1 electron. That gives $2\text{ClO}_3^- + \text{SO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ClO}_2 + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$. Check O: 8 on each side, and charge: -2 on each side, so it balances.

hints: Calculate the oxidation number of Cl in $\text{ClO}_2$, in $\text{ClO}_2^-$ and in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and compare the starting value with the two product values.
walkthrough:
See what disproportionation really means**
Picture one starting substance splitting its fate. The same element in the same starting oxidation state goes two ways at once, one part loses electrons and one part gains electrons.

Apply it to chlorine here**
In $\text{ClO}_2$, O is -2 so Cl is +4. In $\text{ClO}_2^-$, Cl is +3, that is reduction by 1 electron. In $\text{ClO}_3^-$, Cl is +5, that is oxidation by 1 electron. The same +4 Cl has been both oxidised and reduced, so this is disproportionation.

Final answer: Disproportionation is simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same species. Cl in $\text{ClO}_2$ (+4) is both oxidised to +5 in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and reduced to +3 in $\text{ClO}_2^-$.

hints: Split the overall equation into the change $\text{ClO}_2$ to $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and the change $\text{ClO}_2$ to $\text{ClO}_2^-$, deciding which is oxidation and which is reduction.
Remember that in alkaline solution O and H are balanced with $\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and charge is balanced with $\text{e}^-$.
walkthrough:
Separate the two Cl fates**
Keep the two products apart in your mind. One $\text{ClO}_2$ becomes $\text{ClO}_3^-$, Cl +4 to +5, so electrons are lost. The other $\text{ClO}_2$ becomes $\text{ClO}_2^-$, Cl +4 to +3, so an electron is gained.

Build the simple reduction half-equation**
For $\text{ClO}_2$ to $\text{ClO}_2^-$, atoms already balance and charge goes from 0 to -1, so just add one electron: $$\text{ClO}_2 + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}_2^-$$

Build the oxidation half-equation in alkali**
For $\text{ClO}_2$ to $\text{ClO}_3^-$ you need one extra O. In $\text{OH}^-$ solution supply it with $2\text{OH}^-$ and make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the right: $$\text{ClO}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{e}^-$$ Charge balances, -2 on each side, and adding the two half-equations gives the overall disproportionation equation.

hints: Recall which electrode reaction is oxidation (loss of electrons) for Li to $\text{Li}^+$ and which is reduction (gain of electrons) for $\text{I}_2$ to $\text{I}^-$.
Combine the two half-equations so that electrons cancel to get the overall ionic equation.
walkthrough:
Assign oxidation and reduction**
Lithium metal is oxidised when current flows, it loses an electron to form $\text{Li}^+$. Iodine is reduced at the inert electrode, each $\text{I}_2$ molecule gains electrons to form iodide ions.

Cancel electrons for the overall equation**
Multiply the lithium half-equation by 2 so 2 electrons are released to match the 2 electrons needed by iodine: $$2\text{Li} + \text{I}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Li}^+ + 2\text{I}^-$$

hints: Pick out $E^\ominus = +0.54\ \text{V}$ for $\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-$ and $E^\ominus = -3.04\ \text{V}$ for $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}$ and use $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{positive} - E^\ominus_{negative}$.
walkthrough:
Combine the standard potentials correctly**
The more positive half-cell is iodine, the more negative is lithium. Subtract the negative from the positive: $$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode} = 0.54 - (-3.04) = +3.58\ \text{V}$$ The large positive value tells you the cell reaction is highly feasible, ideal for a long life pacemaker battery.

hints: Start from mass of Li and convert to amount in mol using $n = m/M_r$ with $M_r = 6.9$.
Link moles of Li to moles of electrons and then to total charge using $Q = n(\text{e}^-)F$ with $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.
Rearrange $Q = It$ to $t = Q/I$ and substitute $I = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}$ to find time in seconds.
walkthrough:
Convert lithium mass to moles**
Only moles let you count electrons. Use: $$n(\text{Li}) = \frac{m}{M_r} = \frac{0.10}{6.9} = 1.45 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$$

Convert moles of Li to total charge**
Each Li releases 1 electron, so moles of electrons equals moles of Li. Multiply by the Faraday constant: $$Q = nF = (1.45 \times 10^{-2})(96500) = 1399\ \text{C}$$ This is the total charge the 0.10 g can deliver.

Use Q = It to find lifetime**
Current is charge per second, so time is: $$t = \frac{Q}{I} = \frac{1399}{2.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}$$ Give at least 2 significant figures. This huge time, about 1.8 years, shows why the tiny pacemaker current gives such long battery life.
